ADVANCE AGENDA ITEM
  City of Westlake Village
  June 14, 2023
  Agenda Item: Public Hearing No. 1

TO:  Mayor and City Council

FROM:  Rob de Geus, City Manager

SUBJECT: ESTABLISHMENT OF CITYWIDE DEVELOPMENT IMPACT FEES FOR
  RESIDENTIAL  AND  NON-RESIDENTIAL DEVELOPMENT  —
  APPROVAL OF NEXUS STUDY AND CAPITAL IMPROVEMENTS
  PROGRAM; INTRODUCTION OF ORDINANCE NO. 303-23; AND
  ADOPTION OF RESOLUTION NO. 2304-23

OVERVIEW

This report recommends the City Council approve a Nexus Study and Capital
Improvement Program, introduce Ordinance No. 303-23, and adopt Resolution No. 2304-
23 to establish citywide development impact fees (DIFs) for new residential and non-
residential development.

BACKGROUND

In June 2020, the City Council adopted the North Business Park Specific Plan (NBPSP)
to establish a vision and development framework to guide reinvestment in the Specific
Plan area. Chapter 9 of the NBPSP recommends pursuing a variety of strategies to
implement the Plan, including identifying various cost recovery and funding opportunities.
In January 2021, building upon some of the recommended implementation strategies,
Stanley R. Hoffman Associates (SHA) prepared memos discussing three different funding
opportunities for cost recovery and capital improvements related to the anticipated growth
within the NBPSP area: cost recovery fees, DIFs, and a special benefit assessment
district.

On October 27, 2021, City Council considered these three funding opportunities. The City
Council directed staff to schedule a public hearing to consider adopting cost recovery fees
and directed staff to gather additional information regarding the other funding options. On
February 23, 2022, the City Council conducted a public hearing and adopted Resolution
No. 2238-22 to establish cost recovery fees for the NBPSP.

On May 25, 2022, City Council approved a Professional Services Agreement with SHA
to conduct the analysis necessary to establish DIFs and a special benefit assessment
district. This report provides a summary of the process that has been undertaken to

 prepare the proposed DIFs, the proposed maximum allowable DIFs, and the final steps
necessary to establish DIFs.

FINDINGS AND ALTERNATIVES

DIFs are one-time fees that local agencies charge new development to cover the costs
of capital facilities within an area that are needed to provide and maintain an acceptable
level of service. DIFs are intended to cover the costs of new, expanded, or refurbished
public facilities required as a result of new development. Expenditures are allocated to
new development based on its fair share of the demand for new facilities. These fees are
typically charged to new development at the time a building permit is issued. Staff would
note that DIFs cannot be used to fund existing service deficiencies but only those
additional needs arising from new development. Further, DIFs can be used only for capital
improvements and cannot be used to fund ongoing maintenance or operations.

The Mitigation Fee Act (California Government Code Sections 66000 through 66025)
authorizes local agencies to establish and collect fees to cover the share of capital
facilities costs that can be attributed to the service needs of new development as long as
there is a nexus between the improvements to be funded by the fee and the type of
development on which the fee is imposed. SHA has prepared a Nexus Study (Attachment
3) to support the establishment of DIFs, which includes citywide growth projections for
residential and non-residential development, a Capital Improvement Program for current
and projected capital needs, and a proposed fair share allocation of the capital costs to
new residential and non-residential development.

At the outset of the process to establish DIFs, the intent was to limit the fees to
development in the NBPSP area as most new development was expected to occur in that
area. However, the latest data from the Southern California Association of Governments
indicates that there is likely to be commercial growth in other areas of Westlake Village.
Additionally, recent State legislation allows for new residential development to occur on
commercially zoned properties. In light of these factors, the applicability of the fees was
broadened to ensure that all new residential and non-residential development citywide
contributes a fair share allocation of the capital costs that will be needed for the City to
maintain the levels of service currently in place and to adequately support new growth.
Also, pursuant to direction received from the Land Use Committee, the proposed DIFs
would not apply to the replacement or reconstruction of a single-family residence,
including when the replacement or reconstructed residence is larger than the replaced
residence. A complete list of all development that is proposed to be exempted from the
application of the proposed DIFs is provided below –

  1. Any replacement or reconstruction of a dwelling or non-residential structure
  damaged or destroyed by fire or natural causes;
  2. Rehabilitation or remodeling of an existing residential or non-residential use;
  3. Any replacement or reconstruction of an existing single-family dwelling with
  another single-family dwelling, including replacement structures or reconstructed

  4. Additions to an existing single-family structure;

  6. The construction or addition of an accessory dwelling unit.

The Nexus Study establishes a fee schedule to support a range of facilities and
infrastructure capital costs to serve anticipated new growth in five service programs –
Parks and Parkways, General Government, Sidewalk and Pedestrian Safety Facilities,
Intelligent Transportation System, and Police Protection. The following table provides a
summary of the maximum allowable DIFs for each of these subcategories.

The Capital Improvement Program attached to the Nexus Study provides an itemized list
of the capital expenditures that DIFs would fund for each fee category. For the Parks and
Parkways category, the Nexus Study evaluated two different fees: one assuming the
acquisition of new park facilities to maintain existing levels of service, and one assuming
no acquisition of new park facilities. Per direction from the Land Use Committee, the
proposed fee shown here includes costs for the acquisition of new park facilities.

In order to calculate the total DIF for a particular project, each fee category would be
calculated by multiplying the fees listed by the square footage of a new residential or non-
residential development project. The total DIFs owed for a particular project would be the
sum of the calculation of all fee categories.

On May 4, 2022, and December 5, 2022, the Land Use Committee (at that time Mayor
Pro Tem Pearl and Councilmember Honig) reviewed the proposed DIFs, underlying
methodology and assumptions, and provided direction to staff to move forward with
finalizing the Nexus Study. The Committee discussed the scope of the DIFs and whether
fees should be applied to new development citywide or only to new development within
the NBPSP area. Given the anticipated growth projections outside of the NBPSP area,
the Committee expressed support for citywide DIFs as long as the new fees would not
apply to single-family residential development.

 On May 2, 2023, the Land Use Committee (Mayor Pro Tem Davis and Councilmember
Honig) reviewed the proposed fees and discussed whether the Parks and Parkways DIF
should include a park acquisition fee or just a fee for the cost of park improvements. The
Committee directed staff to include the park acquisition fee in the Parks and Parkways
DIF to ensure that any future increases in population do not result in a decrease to the
level of service currently provided to residents of 4.38 acres of parkland per 1,000
residents. The Committee directed staff to bring the proposed new DIFs to the full City
Council for consideration and adoption. If approved, the DIFs would become effective 60
days after the adoption of Ordinance No. 303-23.

FISCAL IMPACT

If new development occurs according to what is forecasted in the Nexus Study, the
projected total revenues for the Parks and Parkways DIF are $7.74 million, the General
Government DIF are $1.30 million, the Sidewalk and Pedestrian Safety Facilities DIF are
$3.43 million, the Intelligent Transportation System DIF are $196,618, and the Police
Protection DIF are $93,114. The projected total revenues for all DIF subcategories would
be $12.76 million which would offset the cost of capital improvements identified in the
Capital Improvement Program. However, the amount to be collected is unknown since
new development may or may not occur as forecasted.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends the City Council approve the Nexus Study and Capital Improvement
Program, waive full reading and introduce Ordinance No. 303-23, and adopt Resolution
No. 2304-23 to establish citywide DIFs for new residential and non-residential
development. If the City Council concurs, the appropriate motion is as follows.

  MOTION:  "I move the City Council approve the DIF Nexus Study and
  Capital Improvement Program, waive full reading and
  introduce Ordinance No. 303-23, and adopt Resolution No.
  2304-23 to establish citywide development impact fees for
  new residential and non-residential development.”

  ROLL CALL:  Yes

  Senior Planner

  THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF WESTLAKE VILLAGE DOES ORDAIN AS
FOLLOWS:

  Section 1. Code Amendment. Article 8 (Building Regulations; Sewage and
Waste) of the Westlake Village Municipal Code is amended by adding a new Chapter 8.11
to read as follows:

  “CHAPTER 8.11.
  DEVELOPMENT IMPACT FEE

8.11.010.  Title.

  This Chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Development Impact
Fee (“DIF”) Ordinance.

8.11.020.  Findings.

  The City Council, having reviewed and considered the study entitled “City
of Westlake Village Citywide Development Impact Fee Nexus Study” (“Nexus Study”)
approved by the City Council on June 14, 2023, finds and determines that:

  A.  In order to effectively implement the Westlake Village General Plan
and North Business Park Specific Plan (“NBPSP”), manage new residential and non-
residential development, and address impacts caused by such development, certain
public facilities must be constructed or acquired, and public equipment must be acquired.

  B.  In order for the City to construct or acquire public facilities and
acquire public equipment, it is necessary to require that all new development bear its fair
share cost of providing the facilities and equipment reasonably needed to serve that
development.

  C.  Development impact fees ("DIF") are created for that purpose.

  D.  As indicated in the Nexus Study, the DIFs can fund the entire share
or a portion of the capital costs associated with constructing or acquiring public facilities
and acquiring public equipment reasonably needed to serve new development, while any
existing deficiencies in public facilities and equipment would need to be funded from other
sources.

  1

   E.  Payment of the DIF does not necessarily mitigate to a level of
insignificance all impacts from new development. Whether impacts associated with a
particular development project have been mitigated to a level of insignificance will be
determined by the City on a case by case basis.

  F.  The public facilities and equipment described in the Nexus Study
include data compiled from information provided by various City departments based on
the anticipated needs of the City due to future development based on the City’s General
Plan and the NBPSP.

  G.  The DIF collected pursuant to this Chapter shall be used toward the
construction and acquisition of public facilities and equipment identified in the Nexus
Study. The need for the public facilities and equipment is related to new residential and
non-residential development because such new development will bring additional people
and other uses into the City thus creating an increased demand for the public facilities
and equipment.

  H.  The cost estimates set forth in the Nexus Study are reasonable cost
estimates for the public facilities and equipment and that portion of the DIF expected to
be generated by new development will not exceed the total fair share of these costs.

  I.  Failure to mitigate growth impacts on public facilities and equipment
within the City will place residents in a condition perilous to their health, safety, and
welfare.

  J.  There is a reasonable relationship between the use of the DIF and
the type of development projects on which the DIF is imposed because the DIF will be
used to construct the public facilities and purchase equipment, and the public facilities
and equipment are necessary for the health and welfare of the residential and non-
residential users of the development projects on which the DIF will be levied.

  K.  There is a reasonable relationship between the need for the public
facilities and equipment and the type of development projects on which the DIF is imposed
because it will be necessary for the residential and non-residential users of the
development projects to have access to the public facilities and equipment in order to
use, inhabit, and have access to the development projects. New development will benefit
from the facilities and equipment to be funded with DIF and the burden of such new
development will be mitigated, in part, by the payment of the DIF.

  L.  This Chapter is for the purpose of promoting public health, safety,
comfort, and welfare, and adopts means that are appropriate to attaining those ends.

8.11.030.  Authority.

  This Chapter is established under the authority of Article 11, Section 7 of
the California Constitution and the Mitigation Fee Act, which provides that a local agency
may establish fees for the purpose of defraying all or a portion of the cost of public facilities
related to development projects.

 8.11.040.  Purpose.

  This Chapter serves the following purposes:

  A.  It establishes and sets forth policies, regulations, and fees relating to
the funding and installation of the public facilities and equipment necessary to address
the direct and cumulative environmental effects generated by new development projects
described and defined in this Chapter.

  B.  It establishes the authorized uses of the DIF collected.

8.11.050.  Administrative Responsibility.

  The City Manager shall be responsible for the administration of this Chapter.
The City Council is authorized to adopt a resolution establishing administrative
procedures for the implementation of this Chapter.

8.11.060.  Definitions.

  For the purposes of this Chapter, unless it is plainly evident from the context
that a different meaning is intended, the following definitions shall apply. Whenever a
reference is made to a law other than this Code, the reference applies to the then-current
version of such law.

  A.  “Accessory Dwelling Unit” shall have the meaning as set forth in
Section 9.2.020 of Chapter 9.2 of Article 9 of this Code.

  B.  “Certificate of Occupancy” means a certificate of occupancy as
defined in the Building Code of the City of Westlake Village or by state law.

  C.  “City” means the City of Westlake Village.

  D.  “City Manager” means the City Manager of the City or his or her
designee.

  E.  “Credit” means a credit allowed pursuant to Section 8.11.100, which
may be applied against the DIF.

  F.  “Development Agreement” means an agreement entered into
between the City and an owner of real property pursuant to Government Code Section
65864 et seq.

  G.  “Development Impact Fees,” “DIF,” or “Fees” means the fees
imposed pursuant to the provisions of this Chapter.

  H.  “Development Project” or “Project” means any project undertaken for
the purpose of development, including the issuance of a permit for construction pursuant
to Article 8.

  K.  “Facilities and Equipment” means the public facilities and equipment
financed by the DIF program and includes all facilities set forth in the Nexus Study and
any subsequent revisions thereof approved by resolution of the City Council, including

  L.  “Final Inspection” means a final inspection as defined in the Building

  M.  “Mitigation Fee Act” means Chapter 5 (commencing with Section

  N.  “Mobilehome” shall have the meaning as set forth in Section 9.2.020

  O.  “Nexus Study” means the “City of Westlake Village Citywide

  P.  “Non-residential Use” means commercial, office, industrial, and other

  Q.  “Residential Use” means single-family and multifamily residential

  R.  “Revenue” or “Revenues” means any funds received by the City

  S.  “Single-Family Dwelling” shall have the meaning as set forth in

  T.  “Structure” shall have the meaning as set forth in Section 9.2.020 of

8.11.070.  Development Impact Fee.

  In order to assist in providing revenue to acquire or construct the public
facilities and equipment set forth in the Nexus Study and to fulfill the purposes of this
Chapter there is hereby established development impact fees to be paid for each

 development project, or a portion thereof, to be constructed in the City. The amount of the
DIF, the description of the facilities and equipment to be financed by DIF, definitions of
terms necessary to implement the DIF, and such other regulations as may be necessary
or convenient to implement and administer the DIF to be imposed pursuant to this Chapter
shall be established by resolution of the City Council.

8.11.080.  Payment of DIF.

  DIF shall be paid as follows:

  A.  DIFs for non-residential uses shall be paid prior to the issuance of a
building permit.

  B.  DIFs for residential uses shall be due and payable in accordance
with California Government Code Section 66007, upon the issuance of a building permit;
provided, however, that the DIFs imposed may be deferred until the date of the final
inspection, or the date the certificate of occupancy is issued, whichever occurs first,
pursuant to a written agreement, entered into and recorded in accordance with California
Government Code Section 66007(c).

  C.  For development projects that the City does not require a final
inspection or issue a certificate of occupancy, the DIF shall be paid prior to any use or
occupancy.

  D.  DIFs shall be assessed one (1) time per lot or parcel except in cases
of changes in land use. DIFs for changes in land use shall be reduced by the amount of
any previously paid DIF for that property. It shall be the responsibility of the applicant to
provide documentation of any previously paid DIF.

  E.  The required DIFs shall be the fee amounts in effect at the time of
payment.

  F.  There shall be no deferment of required DIF payments beyond final
inspection or issuance of certificate(s) of occupancy, except as provided by law.

  G.  Notwithstanding any other written requirements to the contrary, DIFs
shall be paid whether or not the development project is subject to City conditions of
approval imposing the requirement to pay the DIF.

  H.  If all or part of the development project is sold prior to payment of the
DIF, the property shall continue to be subject to the requirement for payment of the DIF
as provided herein.

8.11.090.  Method of Calculating DIF.

  DIFs for residential and non-residential uses shall be calculated in
accordance with the Nexus Study, subject to modification by resolution of the City Council.

 Building areas shall be determined or verified by City staff based upon applicants’ site
plans as submitted to the City.

8.11.100.  Credits.

  If an owner or developer of real property dedicates land or constructs
facilities identified in the applicable fiscal year or five-year City Capital Improvement
Program, the City may grant the owner or developer a credit in one (1) or more of the fee
components described in this Chapter against the DIFs required. No credit shall be
granted for the cost of improvements not defined herein as “facilities and equipment” in
the Nexus Study. A credit granted at the time of development approval shall be included
as a condition of that approval and may be included as a term in a development
agreement for the project. After development approval, but before the issuance of a
building permit, an owner or developer may request a credit from the City Manager. If the
City Manager determines that a credit is appropriate, the owner or developer shall enter
into a credit agreement, which shall be approved by the City Council. The credit amount
shall be initially calculated by estimating the fair market value of the land dedicated or by
estimating the cost of constructing facilities. The City shall subsequently review and
determine the actual value of the land dedicated and the actual construction costs
allowable. Any credit granted shall not exceed the allocated cost for the facilities and
equipment. Any credit granted shall be given in stated dollar amounts only.

8.11.110.  Annual Fee Adjustment.

  Beginning July 1, 2024, the City Manager shall authorize the adjustment of
the DIF rates for inflation on July 1st of each year by the percentage change in the
Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U): Los Angeles-Long Beach-
Anaheim (or any successor index). The calculation for that annual adjustment shall be
made using the month of April over the month of April in the prior year.

8.11.120  Exemptions.

  The following types of construction shall be exempt from the provisions of
this Chapter:

  A.  Any replacement or reconstruction of a dwelling or non-residential
structure damaged or destroyed by fire or natural causes;

  B.  Rehabilitation or remodeling of an existing residential or non-
residential use;

  C.  Any replacement or reconstruction of an existing single-family
dwelling with another single-family dwelling, including replacement structures or
reconstructed structures that exceed the documented total square footage of the original
single-family dwelling;

  D.  Additions to an existing single-family structure;

foundation, on any site; and

  A.  The construction or addition of an accessory dwelling unit.

8.11.130.  Fee Administration.

  All DIF received pursuant to this Chapter shall be deposited, invested,
accounted for, and expended in accordance with California Government Code Section
66006 and all other applicable provisions of law.

8.11.140.  Administrative Costs.

  The costs for administering the provisions of this Chapter shall be recovered
annually using revenues from the DIF program administration fund.”

  Section 2. CEQA. The City Council finds that it can be seen with certainty that
there is no possibility the adoption of this Ordinance may have a significant effect on the
environment because the adoption of this Ordinance establishes development impact
fees and applicable regulations, and no specific development is authorized by the
establishment of DIFs. It is therefore exempt from California Environmental Quality Act
review pursuant to Title 14, Section 15061(b)(3) of the California Code of Regulations.

  Section 3. Severability. If any section, subsection, sentence, clause, phrase
or portion of this Ordinance is for any reason held to be invalid or unconstitutional by the
decision of any court of competent jurisdiction, such decision shall not affect the validity
of the remaining portions of this Ordinance. The City Council declares that it would have
adopted this Ordinance and each section, subsection, sentence, clause, phrase or portion
thereof irrespective of the fact that any one or more sections, subsections, sentences,
clauses, phrases or portions be declared invalid or unconstitutional.

  Section 4. Certification. The City Clerk shall certify to the passage of this
Ordinance and shall cause this Ordinance to be published in the manner prescribed by
law.

   RESOLUTION NO. 2304-23

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
  WESTLAKE VILLAGE APPROVING THE CITYWIDE
  DEVELOPMENT IMPACT FEE NEXUS STUDY DATED
  MAY 25, 2023, ADOPTING A CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT
  PROGRAM AS PART OF THE NEXUS STUDY, ADOPTING
  DEVELOPMENT IMPACT FEES, AND MAKING A
  DETERMINATION OF EXEMPTION UNDER CEQA

  WHEREAS, in adopting Chapter 8.11 of the Westlake Village Municipal Code (the
“Municipal Code”), the City Council established the requirement for the payment of
development impact fees (“DIFs”) by new developments within the City, to ensure that
certain public facilities or capital improvements are constructed and made available
consistent with build-out of the City, in accordance with the City’s General Plan and
concurrent with the need caused by new development; and

  WHEREAS, Chapter 8.11 (“Development Impact Fee”) of the Municipal Code,
provides that the City Council shall, by resolution, establish the amount of the DIF, the
description of the facilities, capital improvements, and equipment to be financed by DIF,
definitions of terms necessary to implement the DIF, and such other regulations as may
be necessary or convenient to implement and administer the DIF to be imposed pursuant
to Chapter 8.11 of the Municipal Code; and

  WHEREAS, Stanley R. Hoffman Associates, Inc. has prepared the City of
Westlake Village Citywide Development Impact Fee Nexus Study dated May 25, 2023
(the “Nexus Study”). The Nexus Study identifies capital projects necessary to meet the
goals, programs, and objectives within the City’s General Plan; and

  WHEREAS, the Nexus Study describes the benefit and impact areas on which
DIFs are to be imposed and collected, describes the reasonable relationship between the
DIFs and the various types of new development, analyzes the need for new public
facilities and improvements which will be necessitated by new development, sets forth a
methodology for determining the relationship between new development, the needed
public facilities and improvements, and the estimated cost of those improvements, and
otherwise satisfies the requirements of the law and Government Code Sections 66000 et
seq. (the “Mitigation Fee Act”), including Assembly Bill (“AB”) 602 (2022) (Gov. Code,
§ 66016.5), with regard to the imposition and collection of DIFs; and

Governments (“SCAG”) for its Regional Transportation Plan (“RTP”) 2024 update, and
provides the basis for calculating and adopting DIFs in the following categories: (1) parks
and recreation capital facilities and equipment, (2) general government capital facilities,

1.2  Mitigation Fee Act General Requirements
The Mitigation Fee Act, which was enacted by AB 1600 (1987) and became effective in 1989, is

 1. Identify the purpose of the fee.

 2. Identify the use to which the fee will be put.

 3. Determine how there is a reasonable relationship between:

  a. The fee’s use and the type of development project on which the fee is imposed.

  b. The need for the public facility and the type of development project on which the fee is

1.5  Methodology
There are different approaches to conducting DIF nexus studies. The primary purpose behind any
approach is to demonstrate a reasonable relationship between the demand impact that new
growth places on local agency services and the costs allocated to this new growth to expand or
refurbish public facilities to maintain acceptable LOS. In the case of an entirely new infrastructure
system, costs are allocated to existing and new development on a fair-share basis. The cost
allocated to new development forms the basis for the DIF, where fees are estimated for each
land use by the relative impacts placed on the service provided.
This Nexus Study utilizes two different approaches to estimate the maximum allowable DIFs –
the Existing Inventory Method and the System Plan Method – as explained below.

 Existing Inventory Method: Estimates the existing cost standards per unit service demand to
fund the expansion or refurbishment of public facilities at the existing LOS provided by the City.
In this Nexus Study, this approach has been used to establish fees for Parks and Recreation
Facilities, General Government Facilities, and Police Protection Facilities.
The Existing Inventory Method allocates costs to new growth based on the ratio of the valuation
of existing public facilities to current demand from existing development. In effect, this method
helps determine the rate of public facility costs per unit of demand upholding current LOS
standards.
Often, employing the Existing Inventory Method is not possible without an extensive survey and
valuation of all assets constituting agency-owned capital facilities. This Nexus Study builds on the
recently completed City of Westlake Village Asset Management Plan (AMP) (2022) that provides
the necessary details on the valuation of capital assets owned by the City for Parks and Parkways
and General Government facilities. The existing cost standards for Police Protection vehicles and
equipment, which the City pays to Los Angeles County (County) pursuant to a contract for police
protection by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department (LASD), are published annually.
Employing the Existing Inventory Method allows the City to make the determination that new
growth will pay its way for the development and expansion of public facilities at the same LOS
standards currently available to existing users in the City. This method results in revenues that
can only be attributed to new growth and separates out any public facility deficiencies, if present,
that impact existing users and would need to be addressed and funded from other sources.
The Existing Inventory Method is often employed when long-term plans for new capital facilities
are yet to be fully determined. Future capital facilities required to serve new development can
be identified on a continuous basis through the City’s capital improvement plan (CIP).
System Plan Method: This approach is adopted when capital expenditures associated with a
proposed infrastructure plan are pre-determined, but whose benefits are shared by both existing
and new development. In this case, the total demand impact from both existing and new users
is used to estimate the cost per unit demand of the planned facility. This enables the allocation
of costs to existing and new users on a fair-share basis. Further, the capital cost share for new
users is allocated by type of development based on their relative demand impact to determine
the DIF on per unit and square foot basis. In this report, this approach has been utilized to
estimate the DIFs for backbone transportation capital projects based on the Sidewalk Master
Plan, Citywide Pedestrian Safety study, and the Intelligent Transportation System (ITS) Master
Plan.

  INTELLIGENT TRANSPORTATION SYSTEM
6.1  Public Facilities Context

The City has developed an Intelligent Transportation System Masterplan that adopts
technological innovations for safety, mobility, and environmental sustainability. ITS technologies
work with traditional infrastructure by integrating advanced communications technologies into
existing backbone infrastructure to improve transportation operations, efficiency, and
reliability. ITS technologies are targeted at infrastructure, vehicles, and travelers, which are
integrated with an intelligent transportation system. The proposed ITS is a completely new city-
wide system with no LOS precedents. According to the masterplan, the City’s vision for ITS is to
provide the following:

  • State of the art technology commensurate with the City’s traffic operations challenges.
  • Reliable, redundant communication.
  • Technology solutions that enable coordinated operations with adjacent jurisdictions and
  emergency responders during emergency events.
  • A cost-effective, safe, and reliable transportation network.

Capital improvements under the ITS will involve upgrading controller assemblies, installing
cameras, upgrading detection systems and battery backup systems, and installing conduit and
fiber optic cable to connect field units to a central system at City Hall.

6.2  ITS Capital Expenditures

The ITS will be a new infrastructure system within Westlake Village, with no precedent. Hardware
and software components will include traffic signal controllers, an Advanced Traffic Management
System (ATMS), CCTV cameras, video management systems, video detection, and
communication infrastructure. The capital cost for ITS is estimated at a total of $3.3 million in
capital expenditures. This new system will serve both existing users and projected new
development within the City. Therefore, capital expenditures have been allocated to existing and
new development on a fair-share basis, as discussed below.

6.3  Cost Allocation and Fee Estimation Methodology

The ITS DIF is calculated by employing the System Plan Method, where the total capital costs
($3.3 million) are divided by the total trips generated by land use from both existing and new
development to determine the overall cost standard per trip. This calculated cost standard allows
for a fair-share allocation of overall ITS system costs to existing and new development based on
their respective share of trips generated. Further, the capital expenditures allocated to new
development forms the basis for the DIF calculation. The cost standard per trip is applied to the

  POLICE PROTECTION

7.1  Public Facilities Context

The City does not have its own police department and contracts with the County for police
protection by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department (LASD). Based on inputs received from
the City Manager’s Office, the LASD’s Contract Law Bureau has confirmed that the deployment
of additional deputies to maintain current LOS due to any additional growth in service demand
from new development will involve ‘common sense startup costs’ to be covered by the City.
These terms are stated in Section 8.1. of the Municipal Law Enforcement Safety (MLES)
Agreement between the County and the City. These include the purchase of vehicles and
equipment to be used by deputies to perform their duties. The County will not be purchasing
these assets as they are additional demands placed on it by the City.

7.2  Service Population

Impact on police protection public facilities is from the City’s residential and non-residential
users, which together constitute the service population to develop the cost standard. The capital
cost standard is based on the current deputy staff time and associated vehicle and equipment
costs that are needed to perform police protection services. The service population calculation
takes into account 100 percent of the current 2022 residential population and weighted 50
percent share of the 2022 total Westlake Village workers living outside the City. The reason for
this 50 percent weighted share, per common practice in public finance analysis, is that employees
in the City do not have an around the clock impact on City infrastructure and services. As shown
in Table 7-1, the service population (city resident population and weighted employment) for
police protection is estimated at 14,931 persons in 2022.
